q: What is a foundation model?
o: A large model pre-trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks
A small model trained for one narrow task only
e: Foundation models (FMs) are pre-trained on huge, varied datasets and then adapted (by prompting, RAG or fine-tuning) to many tasks.

q: What is a token in the context of large language models?
o: A unit of text, such as a word or part of a word, that the model reads and writes
A password used to call the model API
e: Models process text as tokens. Prompts and answers are measured, limited and billed in tokens.
an: Every Oracle reply is billed per token in and out. That's why RPGACE keeps prompts short and caps replies at 3,000 tokens.

q: What are embeddings?
o: Numeric vectors that represent meaning, so similar content sits close together
Compressed copies of the model weights
The system prompt of a chatbot
Encrypted versions of the training data
e: Embeddings map text, images or other data to vectors. Similar meanings have nearby vectors, which powers semantic search and RAG.
an: RPGACE's session memory search matches keywords. Embeddings would let it find 'the time the app froze' even if you typed 'lag' instead.

q: What does the context window of an LLM determine?
o: The maximum amount of text (in tokens) the model can consider at once
How many users can call the model at the same time
The number of layers in the model
How long the model stays deployed
e: The context window is the limit on prompt plus conversation plus answer tokens the model can handle in one go.
an: Bookworm condenses long chapters before sending them, so the important text fits in the window instead of being cut off.

q: Which neural network architecture, built around 'attention', powers modern large language models?
e: Transformers use self-attention to weigh how each token relates to every other token, which made modern LLMs possible.

q: Which type of generative model creates images by starting from random noise and removing it step by step?
e: Diffusion models learn to reverse a noising process, gradually turning noise into an image that matches the prompt.

q: What is a multimodal model?
o: A model that can work with more than one type of data, such as text and images
A model deployed in more than one AWS Region
A model trained by several teams
A model with several output languages
e: Multimodal models take or produce several data types: text, images, audio or video.
an: RPGACE uses one when you photograph a meal and Oracle turns the picture into a food log.

q: A model gives a confident, detailed answer that is factually false. What is this called?
e: Hallucinations are plausible-sounding but incorrect outputs. Grounding with RAG, clear prompts and human review reduce them.
an: Oracle did this when its SELF_KNOWLEDGE went stale: it confidently said Quest Board progress was saved when it wasn't.

q: Which approach most directly reduces hallucinations about a company's own policies?
o: Retrieval-augmented generation using the company's policy documents
Using a bigger context window with no extra data
e: RAG grounds answers in retrieved, trusted documents, so the model doesn't rely on memory alone.

q: Increasing the temperature setting usually makes model output:
e: Higher temperature spreads probability across more token choices, giving more varied output. Lower temperature is more focused and repeatable.

q: A team needs consistent, factual answers for a customer support bot. Which temperature setting is most appropriate?
o: Temperature has no effect on consistency
e: Low temperature reduces randomness, which suits factual, repeatable answers.

q: What does the top-p (nucleus sampling) setting control?
o: The model picks only from the smallest set of likely tokens whose probabilities add up to p
The total number of tokens in the reply
e: Top-p limits choices to the most probable tokens covering probability p. Lower top-p means less varied output.

q: What does the top-k setting control?
o: The model chooses the next token only from the k most likely options
The number of prompts processed in a batch
The length of the context window
e: Top-k restricts sampling to the k highest-probability tokens. Smaller k means more predictable output.

q: Which inference parameter caps how long a model's response can be?
e: Max tokens sets an upper limit on generated output. It does not force the model to use them all.
an: RPGACE raised Oracle's cap from 1,200 to 3,000 tokens after a Visual Treatment reply was cut off mid-document. You're billed only for tokens actually generated.

q: What is a stop sequence?
o: A string that tells the model to stop generating when it appears
A security control that blocks a user
The last layer of a neural network
A command that deletes a model
e: Stop sequences end generation at a chosen marker, useful for structured or templated output.

q: Why can the same prompt give different answers each time?
o: Generative models sample from probabilities, so output is non-deterministic
The model retrains after every request
e: Sampling makes output vary. Lower temperature, top-p and top-k make it more consistent but rarely perfectly identical.

q: Which tasks are generative AI well suited to? (Choose TWO.)
o: Guaranteeing exact calculations for financial audits
Replacing all human review in medical diagnosis
e: Generative AI excels at creating and summarising content. Exact, regulated or safety-critical decisions still need deterministic systems and human oversight.

q: Which is a disadvantage of generative AI solutions?
o: Outputs can be inaccurate and are hard to fully explain
e: Limits include hallucinations, limited explainability, non-determinism, bias and cost at scale.

q: Which describes how large language models generate text?
o: They predict the next token repeatedly, based on the tokens so far
They look up full answers from a fixed database
They copy the most similar web page
They translate the prompt into code and run it
e: LLMs are next-token predictors. Each generated token is added to the input for the next prediction.

q: Which are stages of a foundation model's lifecycle? (Choose TWO.)
e: The FM lifecycle: data selection, model selection, pre-training, fine-tuning, evaluation, deployment and feedback.

q: Most companies building with generative AI start by:
o: Choosing an existing pre-trained foundation model rather than pre-training their own
Pre-training a new model from scratch
e: Pre-training is extremely expensive. Choosing and adapting an existing FM is far cheaper and faster.

q: Which factors should guide the choice of a foundation model? (Choose TWO.)
e: Selection criteria include cost, latency, modality, accuracy for the task, context window, language support, licensing and customisation options.

q: A company needs fast, cheap answers to simple classification prompts at very high volume. Which model choice is most sensible?
o: A smaller, faster model that is good enough for the task
The largest model available, whatever the cost
e: Bigger isn't always better. A smaller model can cut cost and latency when it meets the accuracy bar.
an: RPGACE does this: the cheap Haiku model handles mechanical clean-up, and Sonnet is saved for judgment work.

q: How is on-demand Amazon Bedrock usage generally priced for text models?
o: By the number of input and output tokens processed
By the size of the S3 bucket
e: On-demand Bedrock pricing is per token, with input and output tokens priced separately. Output tokens usually cost more.
